name: Guinea-Bissau Kriyol
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 5 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Andrade, Ernesto d' & Alain Kihm. 2000. Stress in three creoles. In Ernesto d'Andrade, Maria Antónia Mota & Dulce Pereira (eds), Crioulos de base portuguesa, 97-109. Lisboa: Associação Portuguesa de Linguística. (17-page author preprint from the CLUL site via the Internet Archive)
catalog_locator: Preprint section 2 'Lexical stress in K, S, and B': pp. 3 (noun rule, examples (1)-(2)), 4-5 (verb rule, example (3); residue lápis), 6-8 (bambú, kumé; N ntíndi vs N pañá), 10-12 (rules (13) and (15), fn. 13 disyllabic-verb restriction, kásas/kabás, sángra); published pp. 97-109.
catalog_quote: This suggests a very simple rule, for all intents and purposes identical with that which seems to hold in Portuguese, namely: assign stress to the penultimate syllable, unless the ultimate syllable is heavy, in which case it bears stress. A heavy syllable is one that has a realized coda, and the list of possible codas appears to be the same in K and S and in Portuguese, viz. sonorants and approximants (/l/, /r/, /N/, /I/, /U/) and /s/. [p. 3] ... In K and B, in contrast, the syntactic category of the lexical items is a crucial piece of information: nouns are stressed according to their syllable structure; verbs are stressed on their final syllable, irrespective of syllable structure. ... In both groups there will be a residue of nouns that fall outside the rule (e.g., lápis ‘pencil’ in K). [p. 5] ... (15) Heavy syllables attract stress in K iff (a) they constitute the left or right periphery of the phonological word; (b) a left peripheral syllable is left-heavy (from the onset) or a right peripheral syllable is right-heavy (from the coda). [p. 12]
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Nouns (and other non-verbs): stress the penultimate syllable unless the final syllable has a coda (l, r, nasal, glide, s), in which case the final syllable is stressed (plánta 'plant', minjér 'woman'); verbs take final stress regardless of syllable weight (plantá 'to plant', kumé 'to eat', bambú). A phonological word formed by the 1sg clitic N plus a verb with a prenasalized initial consonant shifts stress to that initial 'left-heavy' syllable (N ntíndi 'I understood' vs. N pañá 'I caught').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed by Andrade & Kihm. Chapouto 2014 p. 17 reports Bull 1989 p. 77: trisyllabic nouns stressed on the last syllable carry a secondary stress on the first syllable, and numerals of more than three syllables have main stress on the penult with secondary stress on the first syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: A residue of nouns falls outside the rule (lápis 'pencil', penult despite heavy final; sángra 'hen coop'); plural -s does not make the final syllable heavy (kásas vs. kabás); the initial-stress rule for N + prenasalized verb is stated only for disyllabic verbs. Chapouto 2014 (pp. 41-42, fn. 37, fn. 45) found her Bissau informants conforming to the noun rule but not the verb-final rule (they judged verb stress 'generally penultimate'). Almeida 1991 p. 5 notes that suffixed object pronouns shift stress to the last syllable. Couto 1994 (per Chapouto) entertains a tonal contour for traditional creole.
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical (word) stress; the authors abstract away from its phonetic realization (intensity/pitch/duration), referring to Kihm & Laks 1989 for that. Domain is the phonological word, which includes the proclitic N 'I' and enclitic object pronouns.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement (Andrade & Kihm 2000, 'K') describes Guinea-Bissau Kriyol proper, i.e. the Bissau-based standard variety (language-level uppe1455; Glottolog dialect biss1249 Bissau-Bolama Creole). The Casamance/Ziguinchor dialect (cach1242 Cacheu-Ziguinchor Creole) is described separately by Biagui & Quint (APiCS ch. 34) as having lexically distinctive stress on the final, penultimate or antepenultimate syllable, so the two varieties should not be merged under one stress reading without checking Biagui 2012. Chapouto 2014's Bissau informants also disputed verb-final stress.

new_statements.quote: p. 105: "pour les noms et les adjectifs, le domaine de l'accent est limité aux deux dernières syllabes; si l'ultième est lourde, elle attire l'accent. Le kriyol peut donc être considéré comme une langue à accent quasi-fixe. Sa règle de placement, semblable à celle du portugais, est sensible à la quantité. Ainsi, l'accent porte sur la pénultième si l'ultième est de type CV (légère), sur l'ultième si elle est de type CVC (lourde)" ; p. 108: "Les noms et les adjectifs sont accentués sur l'ultième si elle est lourde, autrement sur la pénultième. Un écho sur l'initiale des polysyllabes (de longueur trois et plus) est possible, mais non régulier. Les verbes, dont l'ultième est toujours légère, sont accentués sur l'initiale. Un écho de force variable apparaît sur la finale des polysyllabes."
new_statements.translation: p. 105: 'for nouns and adjectives, the stress domain is limited to the last two syllables; if the ultima is heavy, it attracts the stress. Kriyol can therefore be considered a language with quasi-fixed stress. Its placement rule, similar to that of Portuguese, is quantity-sensitive. Thus stress falls on the penult if the ultima is CV (light), on the ultima if it is CVC (heavy)'; p. 108: 'Nouns and adjectives are stressed on the ultima if it is heavy, otherwise on the penult. An echo on the initial syllable of polysyllables (three syllables or more) is possible but not regular. Verbs, whose ultima is always light, are stressed on the initial syllable. An echo of variable strength appears on the final syllable of polysyllables.'

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the existing Andrade & Kihm 2000 statement for nouns/adjectives (penult unless the final syllable is heavy, then final = weight-sensitive, Portuguese-like) and adds detail: two-syllable window, 'quasi-fixed' typology, echo/secondary stresses, plural -s inert, lexical-stratum exceptions. The catalog record itself has an empty rule, so nothing in the catalog is contradicted; the nou…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Kriyol is a stress (not tone) language with one culminative prominence per accentual unit (p. 101). Core creole vocabulary: nouns and adjectives take stress within a final two-syllable window, on the ultima if it is closed/heavy (coda N, r, l, y, w, s; nasal vowels count as V+N, hence heavy), otherwise on the penult (kása, kadéra vs kacúr, korsón, kalabús). Verbs (always light-final) are stressed on the initial syllable: disyllables (kórta), derived trisyllables keep initial stress and are proparoxytone (kánbanta), African-lexicon verbs initial (lánbu, jókoni); verb stress and echo are ultimately fixed at the level of the whole phrase (clitics, aspect markers, negation). Stress is predictable and need not be written except for a few lexemes (pp. 94, 108).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stresses are analysed as echoes of the main stress, predictable from it (p. 101): an optional echo on the initial syllable of nouns of three or more syllables (àplikasón, pùrgisúzu, p. 105); in polysyllabic verbs a variable-strength echo on the final syllable (p. 107-108).
new_statements.exceptions: lapis /'lapis/ and arvuri /'arvuri/ (penult/initial stress despite heavy ultima or against the rule) belong to a lusitanised register (p. 106); recent 'European' (learned Portuguese) loans and 'African' loans (ncit, kon, Noroto, ololo) are often exceptions to the placement rule (p. 106-107); plural /-(V)s/ never shifts stress because it does not assign weight (bajúda/bajúdas, kacúr/kacúrs ~ kacúris, pp. 105-106); non-derived creole trisyllabic verbs (prokura) show instrumentally ambiguous initial-vs-final prominence (p. 107).
new_statements.identity_note: Kihm & Laks 1989 describe the central (Bissau) variety of Guinea-Bissau Kriyol from one Bissau-born native speaker of Manjaku parentage (p. 94) = uppe1455. Silom 2023 (abstract only) studies Kriyol as spoken by Fula speakers in Bafatá and Balanta speakers in Quinara (regional/L2 Guinea-Bissau Kriyol), still uppe1455; the Casamance (Ziguinchor) variety treated by Biagui and APiCS 34 is a separate glottocode (cach1242) and is not among this item's works.

readall_conflicts: Nouns and adjectives: all opened sources agree (Kihm & Laks 1989 pp. 105, 108; Andrade & Kihm 2000; Chapouto 2014's summary and corpus): stress on the penult unless the final syllable is heavy (closed by N, r, l, glide or s), then final, i.e. a Portuguese-like quantity-sensitive right-edge rule. Verbs are the one point of disagreement: Kihm & Laks 1989 (instrumental, one Bissau speaker) analyse verbs as INITIAL-stressed (kórta, kánbanta, lánbu) with a variable echo on the final syllable and phrase-level conditioning, while Andrade & Kihm 2000 state that Kriyol verbs bear FINAL stress irrespective of syllable structure (with stress retraction to the initial syllable of disyllabic prenasalised-onset verbs after the clitic N); Chapouto 2014 reports her informants stress verbs mostly on the penult, which for the disyllabic majority coincides with the 1989 initial-stress analysis. Silom 2023 could not be read beyond its abstract and takes no position.

sources.citation: Biagui, Noël Bernard & Nicolas Quint. 2013. Casamancese Creole. APiCS Online survey chapter 34.
sources.note: Section 4: 'Casamancese Creole is a stress language. Each content word has a stressed syllable.. (1) final: kortá.. (2) penultimate: kárgu.. (3) antepenultimate: lárguma.. Stress has a distinctive function: kónta "(pearl) necklace" vs. kontá "tell"'; open stressed penults are lengthened phonetically. This is the Ziguinchor dialect (Glottolog cach1242).
